options: Render `plan`, show a field-level fallback for `name`, and flag that upstream: the operation ran and one nullable field did not.
Discard the payload and show the page-level error state: a non-empty `errors` array means at least one selected field is invalid, so `data` cannot be trusted.
Refetch the whole query once, and when `errors` persists render both `name` and `plan` empty, because a partial object cannot be rendered consistently.
Render `errors[0].message` in the banner, because `extensions` is an open map any server may leave empty, so the message is the only guaranteed channel.
mcqs.explanation: A GraphQL response reports two independent things: whether the server executed the operation (the HTTP status) and how each selected field resolved (the payload), so `data` next to `errors` is a normal success-with-a-failed-field. Here `data` is non-null, which means the operation ran; `name` is nullable and its resolver failed, so the field came back as `null` and `errors[0].path` points at exactly that field. The client policy therefore follows the payload: render what resolved, fall back on the failed field, and repair at that field's granularity. The contrast case is the mechanism worth naming — if `name` had been declared non-null, the failure would bubble to the nearest nullable parent and `data` itself (not one field) would come back `null`; that is when a page-level error is the right answer. The strongest distractor is the refetch-and-blank option: refetching is a defensible reflex, but blanking `plan` discards a field that resolved fine, and against a persistently failing upstream it turns a degraded render into an empty one while paying for the whole query again. The discard option confuses one failed nullable field with an untrustworthy payload, which is the confusion the response model exists to prevent. The message option branches on display copy: `message` is human text that changes with any copy edit, while `extensions.code` is where a stable, branchable code belongs (https://graphql.org/learn/response/).

mcqs.question: A worker retries whatever call ends with a timeout or a connection reset, using the same code path for every endpoint. Which of these four calls can it retry automatically without any extra coordination?
options: `GET /invoices?after=eyJvIjo0MH0&limit=50` — the connection died before any response headers arrived.
`POST /payments`, whose helper calls `crypto.randomUUID()` inside each attempt so every try ships a fresh `Idempotency-Key`.
`POST /invoices/8f2/resend`, which mails the customer another copy and has no dedupe server-side.
`POST /orders`, with a server-assigned id and no key, on the assumption that a 5xx means nothing was created.
mcqs.explanation: Retry safety is a property of the request, not of the failure: a timeout only tells you the response was lost, never what the server did. `GET` is safe, so repeating it cannot change state and an automatic retry is fine even with the outcome unknown. A `POST` needs an idempotency key the server stores next to the result, or a dedupe rule of its own. The strongest distractor is the fresh-key payment, because it looks protected — and that is exactly why it ships: a key names one logical operation (`this payment`), so minting a new one per attempt makes every retry a different operation, the server has nothing to match, and the charge lands twice. The resend option is a genuine side effect too: two deliveries mean two emails the customer may act on. The last option repeats the '5xx means it did not commit' myth — a 5xx can arrive after the write is durable, so the retry creates a second order (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2, https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests).

options: `type`, because RFC 9457 makes the type URI the problem type's primary identifier, stable across occurrences and languages.
`title`, because the RFC keeps it stable per `type`, so two responses that share a `title` are the same kind of problem.
`instance`, because it uniquely identifies the problem occurrence, so the client can key its handling off that URI.
`status`, because it carries the HTTP code in machine-readable form and is what survives a proxy that rewrote the response.
mcqs.explanation: RFC 9457 §3.1.1 requires consumers to use the `type` URI as the problem type's primary identifier, which is what makes the current branch wrong at the root: `detail` is per-occurrence human text (§3.1.4), so a copy change or a negotiated language breaks a match that was never a contract. `type` stays `https://api.example.com/problems/invalid-email` through both, so the client keeps working and can map each type to its own handling. The strongest distractor is `title`: §3.1.3 really does keep it stable per problem type, so someone who read that paragraph and stopped there will pick it — but stability is not identification. `title` is advisory display text, it changes under localization, and two distinct problem types are free to share one, so it cannot key client logic. `instance` fails for the opposite reason: §3.1.5 makes it unique per occurrence, the handle support wants in a log, not a kind. `status` only carries the HTTP class, and every validation problem here is `422`, which is precisely how email and tax-id failures ended up on the same branch. The fix is `type` for the kind plus the problem type's documented extension — for example `errors[].pointer` — to find the field (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html).

options: The client fabricates a cursor from row fields instead of echoing `next_cursor`; a cursor marks a position in the server's model, not a set of columns.
The client re-encodes with `btoa` before `encodeURIComponent`, so base64 padding is percent-escaped and the server decodes a different position.
The client should rebuild the cursor from `id` alone, because `created_at` repeats and equal timestamps are what skip and repeat rows.
Nothing is wrong on the client: adding a snapshot marker to the cursor encoding is a breaking change the API should have versioned.
mcqs.explanation: A cursor marks a position inside the server's ordering, and the client's only obligations are to store it untouched and hand it back; the GraphQL pagination guidance recommends base64 exactly so that nobody starts reading the bytes, and lists 'change how the backend paginates' as the benefit opaque cursors buy. This helper ignores `next_cursor` and rebuilds one from `created_at` and `id`, so the position it requests is defined by the row it happens to hold, not by the snapshot the server encoded; once the encoding carries a snapshot marker the fabricated token no longer describes the same position, rows move between pages, and nothing throws because no request is malformed. The strongest distractor is 'the format change is the server's breaking change', because it is exactly the shape of what people see: a cursor is opaque by contract, so changing its encoding is the evolution clients are supposed to survive — the change exposed the violation, it did not create it. The tiebreaker option is the other near miss: a unique tiebreaker such as `(created_at, id)` belongs to the server's keyset ordering, and a client cannot repair an opaque token by sorting differently. The base64/padding option describes a real bug class, but it yields rejected or undecodable cursors, not silently shifted pages (https://graphql.org/learn/pagination/).

mcqs.question: What is the safest server behavior for a repeated idempotency key with different parameters?
options: Execute the new request and overwrite the old result
Return the original result while silently ignoring differences
Reject the reuse as a parameter mismatch
Generate a new key on behalf of the client
mcqs.explanation: A key represents one logical operation, so different parameters indicate misuse and should be rejected. The best distractor is returning the old result silently: it hides a client bug and makes the caller believe the new parameters were applied.

mcqs.question: Two services your team owns exchange a high-volume market-data feed. The consumer needs server streaming, a deadline and cancellation per call, and generated clients in Go and Kotlin. Which argument actually supports choosing gRPC here?
options: Protobuf is binary and therefore always faster than JSON, so gRPC wins on any service-to-service call.
Both sides are a controlled boundary, and .proto-generated clients plus deadlines and streaming solve a measured problem.
gRPC removes the need for a schema, so the two teams can evolve payloads without contract review.
gRPC is callable directly from browsers over HTTP/2, so the same endpoint can also serve the web dashboard.
mcqs.explanation: The decision checks caller, browser reachability, observability, compatibility workflow, deadlines and streaming — and here gRPC's actual wins apply: one .proto generates both clients, and deadlines, cancellation and streaming are native instead of bolted on. The strongest distractor is the blanket speed claim: protobuf messages are more compact, but latency depends on the workload, and gRPC costs code-generation and deployment tooling that only pays off for a measured problem (https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/introduction/). The browser-reachability claim fails too: browsers cannot speak raw gRPC, which is why a gRPC-Web or transcoding proxy sits at the edge (https://github.com/grpc/grpc-web).

mcqs.question: A client must clear the optional `nickname` and change one element of the `tags` array on `PATCH /users/123`. The endpoint accepts `application/merge-patch+json`. Which statement is correct?
options: `tags` merges element by element, so sending only the changed element appends it without touching the rest of the array.
`null` is stored as a literal JSON null, so removing the member requires a full `PUT` of the resource.
`nickname: null` clears the member, but `tags` is replaced as a whole; element-level tag edits need another patch format, such as JSON Patch.
`PATCH` is idempotent by HTTP method semantics, so the update needs no `If-Match` precondition against concurrent writers.
mcqs.explanation: RFC 7396 defines an object-shaped patch: omitted members stay untouched, a `null` member deletes, and any array or scalar value replaces the target member wholesale — so the array cannot be edited positionally, and the right move is a format that expresses the operation instead of sending ambiguous partial JSON. The strongest distractor is the element-wise merge: it reads "merge" as a deep merge, but Merge Patch recurses only into objects, never into arrays. The `If-Match` distractor is the other common confusion: `PATCH` is not idempotent in general, which is exactly why an entity-version precondition belongs in this request (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7396, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6902).

mcqs.question: A webhook handler lets the framework parse the JSON body, then recomputes the HMAC over `JSON.stringify(parsed)` and compares it with the received signature. It passes locally, but in production roughly 2% of genuine deliveries are rejected. What is the primary cause?
options: The comparison uses `!==` instead of a constant-time compare, so timing noise makes some valid signatures fail.
HMAC must hash the parsed object rather than a string, so the bug is that `JSON.parse` runs before `createHmac`.
Providers rotate the signing secret frequently, so a small share of deliveries is signed with the previous secret.

Re-serializing the parsed body does not reproduce the signed bytes — key order, whitespace, unicode escaping and number formatting differ — so the MAC must be verified over the raw body before parsing.
mcqs.explanation: A signature covers exact bytes, and parsing then re-stringifying is a lossy round trip: member order, whitespace, `\u` escapes and number forms such as `1.0` versus `1` change, so the recomputed MAC diverges whenever the sender serialized differently. Capture the raw body first, verify, then parse. The strongest distractor is the constant-time one: a non-constant comparison is a genuine defect because it leaks timing information, but it never turns a matching MAC into a mismatch, so it cannot explain intermittent rejections (https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/validating-webhook-deliveries, https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks).

scenarios.prompt:
A checkout helper has been in production for a quarter, and four symptoms keep coming back in reviews:

- About 1 in 60 captured payments is charged twice, always on flaky mobile connections; support refunds the duplicate by hand.
- One malformed payload from a partner integration produces roughly 300 POSTs per checkout attempt before the call gives up.
- p99 for the call is 30 s, and when it finally throws the UI says "payment failed" — a handful of those "failed" payments exist in the provider dashboard, and the customer pays again.
- During a five-minute provider outage our workers push several hundred requests per second at the endpoint.

This function is the entire retry policy. Name each defect with the symptom it causes, then rewrite it so retries are safe, bounded, and honest about an outcome nobody knows.

code.caption: The whole policy: one loop, one wall-clock budget, one key per attempt.

rubric: Names the per-attempt key as the cause of the duplicate charges and moves key creation out of the loop, keeping one key per logical payment across retries and across a page reload.
Replaces the blanket retry with a classifier — transport errors, 408/429 and selected 5xx only — and returns 4xx validation and authorization to the caller instead of retrying them.
Bounds the policy with a maximum attempt count, a deadline enforced on the in-flight request (AbortSignal), exponential backoff with jitter, and Retry-After when present.
Treats 409 or an in-progress key as 'someone owns this operation', not as failure, and surfaces an indeterminate state with a reconciliation path instead of throwing 'payment failed'.
States that the guarantee also depends on the server reserving the key atomically and storing key, fingerprint and result, so the client cannot promise exactly-once on its own.

scenarios.prompt: This handler is the only entry point for a payment provider's webhooks. In production: some legitimate deliveries get a 400; the same refund is applied twice after every deploy; two deliveries of one event arriving in parallel both apply; and the provider marks the endpoint slow and keeps retrying. Name each defect with the failure it causes, then rewrite the receiver so signature verification, replay rejection, deduplication and acknowledgement are correct.
rubric: Verifies the HMAC over the raw request bytes before parsing, with a signed timestamp inside a tolerance window and a constant-time comparison.
Persists the provider event id with a unique constraint before any side effect, so retries, redeploys and parallel deliveries deduplicate atomically across instances.
Acknowledges only after durable acceptance (for example 202 after commit plus enqueue) and processes asynchronously with bounded retries and a dead-letter path.
Handles out-of-order or stale events by entity version or by refetching current state instead of assuming delivery order.
Explains that a duplicate still gets a success response without redoing the work, and distinguishes rejected, duplicate and stale deliveries in monitoring.
